newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China tells British--let PLA in HK before handover.
newsitem.headline: China tells British--let PLA in HK before handover.

text.p: China, in a move sure to upset Britain, said on Thursday the People's Liberation Army should enter Hong Kong before the formal sovereignty transfer so soldiers can be in position by midnight June 30.
A major wrangle built up as the British garrison swiftly rejected any idea that more Chinese troops should enter before the handover in 19 days, declaring it alone remains responsible.
China has already sent an advance party of 200 soldiers to prepare garrison, supply and communications facilities. Britain insisted they be unarmed and wear uniforms only in barracks.

Beijing's demand looked certain to widen a breach between China and Britain, which along with the United States, is to boycott the inauguration of an unelected provisional legislature to replace Hong Kong's democratically elected parliament.

"China's People's Liberation Army should be in Hong Kong barracks before the zero hour on July 1 so that after the completion of the handover ceremony they can take up defence responsibilities," Beijing-controlled newspapers said.
The press quoted China's official spokesman in Hong Kong, Zhang Junsheng.
His statement to Ta Kung Pao and Wen Wei Po was the latest sign that China is harrying Britain behind the scenes over the timing of the future PLA garrison's entry on to Hong Kong soil.
Britain hands Hong Kong back to China in a midnight ceremony on June 30, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
Its garrison said Britain alone remained responsible for Hong Kong's defence up to the last minute and there was no need for the PLA garrison to cross over before that moment.
"Britain is not agreeing to the deployment of the main PLA Garrison of Hong Kong before July 1," Ruth Vernon, a spokeswoman for the garrison, told Reuters.

Zhang, deputy chief and official spokesman of China's Hong Kong mission, the Xinhua News Agency branch, said the 1984 Sino-British handover treaty stipulated the PLA would take over the defence of Hong Kong from the stroke of midnight on June 30.
He said China and Britain were discussing details such as the size and timing of the main unit to move into Hong Kong.
Earlier, Wen Wei Po blasted Britain for not letting the PLA troops move into Hong Kong early.

"The British forces believe it will take them two or three hours to complete their withdrawal from Hong Kong (at the time of the handover). But it refuses to let the PLA move into their barracks early. This is unfair," Wen Wei Po said.
Britain's last garrison members are flying out of Hong Kong -- in civilian clothes -- three hours after the handover on a chartered jumbo jet.

A report by the British Broadcasting Corporation on Wednesday night said China wanted troops to arrive before the handover moment with guns and armour in tow, but a British military spokesman said he knew of no such plan.
Beijing has said the size of the PLA Garrison, which will be made up of ground, naval and air forces, will be no more than Britain's troop strength in its heyday -- some 10,000 personnel.

In an unconfirmed report a Hong Kong newspaper said on Wednesday China would send in 6,000 troops to garrison Hong Kong on July 1, with 2,000 crossing over at midnight June 30 and the rest streaming in during the early hours of July 1.
For China, the PLA's arrival will be the most important visible symbol of its restored sovereignty over the territory it lost to Britain in the 19th century opium trade wars.

But many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people view the PLA with alarm because of its "butcher image" resulting from the communist army's bloody crackdown on student-led democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.

These worries were aggravated earlier this week by a strident comment in a Chinese military newspaper, the Defence Daily, calling for a firm hand to stamp out opposition in Hong Kong to planned restrictions on civil liberties after July 1.
"This has made clear just in time that the timebomb buried by (the British) must be dug out, otherwise Hong Kong will never find peace," the paper said.
